title: Jeremiah 11:18–23
context: Jeremiah learns from the LORD that men of his hometown Anathoth (compare 1:1) are plotting to kill him to stop his prophesying. He describes himself as “a gentle lamb that is led to the slaughter,” an image also found in Isaiah 53:7; the two passages are named here without merging them. Jeremiah commits his cause to the LORD who “tests the heart and the mind” (11:20, compare 20:12). The LORD answers (11:21–23) with a word of judgment on the men of Anathoth. Jeremiah 12:6 later reveals that even his own family dealt treacherously with him. Both traditions read the passage as an honest record of a persecuted prophet’s prayer, and they read his request for vengeance as handing judgment to God rather than taking it himself.

verses.text: The LORD gave me knowledge of it, and I knew it. Then you showed me their doings.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says the LORD gave him knowledge of the plot, so that he knew it. Arminian readers see God protecting his servant by revealing hidden danger, giving him what he needed to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s care for the prophet, unveiling the schemes of his enemies. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as God’s watchful protection of a faithful messenger who would otherwise have been unaware.

verses.text: But I was like a gentle lamb that is led to the slaughter. I didn’t know that they had devised plans against me, saying, “Let’s destroy the tree with its fruit, and let’s cut him off from the land of the living, that his name may be no more remembered.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says he was like a gentle lamb led to slaughter, unaware of the plan to cut him off. Arminian readers note his vulnerability and innocence, and the image also found in Isaiah 53:7.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the Isaiah image and see Jeremiah’s suffering as part of a pattern of faithful servants who suffer. Both traditions name the parallel without merging the two passages, reading Jeremiah’s words first in their own setting.

verses.text: But, LORD of Armies, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind, I will see your vengeance on them; for to you I have revealed my cause.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah appeals to the LORD of Armies, who judges righteously and tests heart and mind, and commits his cause to him. Arminian readers see trust placed in God’s fair judgment rather than in personal revenge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an appeal to God who searches the inner life, compare 20:12 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the request for vengeance as handing judgment to God, an honest prayer that leaves the outcome in his hands.

verses.text: “Therefore the LORD says concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, saying, ‘You shall not prophesy in the LORD’s name, that you not die by our hand’—
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks concerning the men of Anathoth, who threaten Jeremiah with death if he keeps prophesying. Arminian readers note the painful fact that opposition comes from his own hometown, those who knew him best.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as showing the cost of faithful prophecy, which provokes hostility even from neighbors. Both traditions read the threat as an attempt to silence God’s word, a pattern later echoed in Jeremiah’s own family (compare 12:6).

verses.text: therefore the LORD of Armies says, ‘Behold, I will punish them. The young men will die by the sword. Their sons and their daughters will die by famine.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says he will punish them: young men by sword and children by famine. Arminian readers see judgment answering those who sought to kill the messenger and silence God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God defending his word and his servant through judgment on the persecutors. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, as God’s answer to violent opposition, without delighting in the suffering described.

verses.text: There will be no remnant to them, for I will bring evil on the men of Anathoth, even the year of their visitation.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says there will be no remnant for the men of Anathoth in the year of their visitation. Arminian readers note the severity of the sentence and read it within the wider judgment on Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the year of visitation as God’s appointed time of reckoning for the plotters. Both traditions read the unit as an honest record of a persecuted prophet and God’s defense of him, and they note that men of Anathoth later return from exile (compare Ezra 2:23).
